artifacts.notes:
WHAT THIS IS: uncorrected optical character recognition of a whole English lay missal, 36,485 LF-terminated lines, valid UTF-8, no CR bytes, landed as a plain source artifact and nothing more. It is deliberately NOT structured as liturgical records; the prior lt-hist corpus cut the same text into six markdown 'sections' bounded by line ranges over the downloaded file, and reproducing that shape here would reproduce a defect with better provenance attached. Addressability by identity belongs to passage records with real loci over these exact bytes. Until such a passage exists this artifact is a finding aid.

OCR QUALITY. Measured here by scripts/_ocr_quality.py at an English function-word share of 0.3149 over 225,027 tokens, Latin 0.0339, classified `prose-english`. The two figures must be read together: the Ordinary and Canon print Latin beside English, and a large part of the book is calendar and index matter that is neither, so the English share is a floor rather than a ceiling on the prose. The damage is the ordinary damage of a 2006 scan of small-type letterpress with the long s: `fuch of the Laity` and `MifTal` for such of the Laity and Missal at lines 33 and 34, `Poflcommunion`, `Semidoublc`, and Latin words worse used than English ones -- `fupp- / liciter` broken across lines, `rogamu.?` for rogamus at line 2875 and `Kcclesia` for Ecclesia at line 2881. Quote from this artifact only through a checked passage, and do not rest a negative search on it: the raw-line modes establish absence of a string, not absence of a text. TWO NEGATIVE SEARCHES THAT ARE ARTEFACTS AND NOT FINDINGS, named so nobody repeats them. The strings `Keating` and `1806` both return zero hits in this file, the first because the title-page imprint is optically destroyed and the second because the printed year was not captured at all; neither absence says anything about the book.

WHAT THE TEXT LAYER CONTAINS AND WHERE. The introduction explaining the book's use to the laity opens at line 33; the note attributing the Epistles, Lessons and Gospels to the Rheims and Douay version as revised by Challoner stands at lines 109 to 113, and the table of abbreviations with the pre-1911 grades at lines 115 to 123; the calendar with the English proper saints runs from about line 158, St George as patron of England at the first class at line 269 and St Augustine the apostle of England at line 320; the Ordinary is headed from line 1283; the Canon of the Mass is present entire in facing columns, headed at line 2868 and opening at line 2871 with `TE igitur clementissi- / me^Pater, per Jesum / Christum` against `WE humbly pray / and beseech thee, / therefore, most merciful / Father` from line 2894; and the proper Masses begin at line 3987.

IDENTITY. Internet Archive item a550137400unknuoft, scanned in 2006 on a Scribe station at 600 ppi from a copy contributed by Saint Mary's College of California under the Toronto collection, sponsored by the National Institute for Newman Studies; 744 page images, page_number_confidence 87. Its catalogue record supplies creator `Catholic Church`, publisher `London : P. Keating, Brown` and date 1806, and links OpenLibrary edition OL13990585M. The publisher line is the catalogue's conflation of two names the book keeps apart: P. Keating published it and Brown and Co. printed it, per the title page and the final leaf respectively. See the edition record.
artifacts.rights_basis: Public domain in the United States because the book was first published outside the United States before the pre-1931 line, and on that ground alone. THE LINE, AND THE YEAR IT WAS DERIVED FOR. Any work first published abroad before 1931 is out of United States copyright; that is the line guidance/missals.md records from Cornell's public-domain chart as current on 1 January 2026, correcting the commissioning brief's 'before 1930'. THE LINE MOVES EVERY JANUARY, which guidance/missals.md:249 states in terms, so it is written here as derived for calendar year 2026 and not as a standing rule: on 1 January 2027 it becomes before 1932, and a later reader must re-derive it rather than quote this sentence. Publication in 1806 clears the line by a hundred and twenty-five years, and the margin survives the fact that the book's own printed year has not been read from the bytes: the edition record explains that 1806 is the cataloguer's date, and any London printing by this publisher at this address is of the early nineteenth century, so the ground holds under any reading of the year that the evidence permits. THE SCAN AND ITS TEXT LAYER ADD NOTHING FOR ANYONE TO OWN. A faithful mechanical reproduction of a public-domain work is not original authorship (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y. 1999)), and machine optical character recognition adds no human authorship on top of it: this text layer was produced autonomously by the Internet Archive's ABBYY pipeline in its 2006 Scribe workflow and converted by abbyy-to-hocr 1.1.7 per the item's own `ocr_converted` field, and there is no author to hold a right in it. NOT RELIED ON, EXPRESSLY: that the Internet Archive item is available, that the download succeeded, or that the host marks it public domain. guidance/sources.md:395-400 holds that availability and successful download are insufficient for `tracked`, and the item's public-domain licence URL was the whole of the prior lt-hist corpus's ground for this book -- the ground refused at src/sources/inventories/lt-hist-rights-audit-v1.toml, and the same kind of ground that corpus used to import the 2011 Roman Missal. The mark is recorded as a fact about the item and is not a link in this basis, which would be unchanged if the item carried no mark or a contradictory one. NO THIRD-PARTY DIGITISATION CLAIM ARISES HERE, and this is worth saying because it is what separates this book from its 1843 sibling. The scan was made by the Internet Archive itself on a Scribe station in 2006, sponsored by the National Institute for Newman Studies from a copy contributed by Saint Mary's College of California; there is no Google front matter, no usage-guidelines leaf, and no scanner-asserted claim anywhere in the bytes, which a search of the whole file for `google`, `copyright`, `all rights reserved` and `creative commons` confirms returns nothing.

work.author: Catholic Church, in an anonymous English translation published by P. Keating, Duke Street, Grosvenor Square, London
work.description: An English lay hand missal of the English mission, giving the Masses of the Roman Missal for a layperson following the Mass. Its Ordinary and its Canon stand in facing Latin and English columns; its Epistles, Lessons and Gospels are, by its own introduction, taken from the Rheims and Douay version as revised by Richard Challoner, so its scriptural English is not the compiler's; the orations and the remaining English are anonymous and unattributed. Its sanctoral is that of the English vicariates, keeping St George as patron of England at the first class, St Augustine the apostle of England and St Edward with octaves, and St Cuthbert, St Dunstan, St Alban proto-martyr, the Venerable Bede, St Winefrid and St Thomas of Canterbury in place. Its introduction directs the reader to the Laity's Directory for the year's variable observance, so it is a book made to be used with an annual ordo rather than to be complete in itself. IT IS A DEVOTIONAL COMPANION AND NOT AN OFFICIAL LITURGICAL TRANSLATION, and its rubrics are those in force long before the 1911, 1955 and 1960 reforms -- it grades feasts as double of the first and second class, greater double, double and semidouble. It stands beside the three sibling hand-missal families in this library, the Cummiskey, Husenbeth and Lefebvre books, and like them its only common object with them is the Latin Missal itself; whether its English of the orations is the same anonymous translation as the Philadelphia Cummiskey missals' has not been collated and must not be assumed from the shared title formula.
work.title: The Roman Missal for the use of the laity, containing the Masses appointed to be said throughout the year
